lesson.title: Water's Special Journey: Understanding Osmosis and Tonicity
lesson.summary: Osmosis is the diffusion of water itself across a selectively permeable membrane, and the direction it moves, driven by differences in solute concentration, determines whether a cell swells, shrinks, or stays stable.
lesson.body:
Osmosis is a specific and especially important case of the diffusion covered in the previous chapter: it is the net movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane, moving from a region of lower solute concentration toward a region of higher solute concentration. Framed in terms of water itself rather than the solutes dissolved in it, water moves from where it is more concentrated, meaning fewer dissolved solutes are taking up space, toward where it is less concentrated, meaning more dissolved solutes are present, which produces the same net effect as saying water follows its own concentration gradient, exactly the passive transport logic established two chapters back.

Because cells are full of dissolved solutes, ions, sugars, proteins, and are bounded by the selectively permeable plasma membrane covered earlier in this unit, the concentration of solutes outside a cell relative to inside determines which way water moves and what happens to the cell as a result. Biologists describe this relationship using three terms. A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the inside of the cell, so water moves into the cell by osmosis. A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the inside of the cell, so water moves out of the cell. An isotonic solution has an equal solute concentration on both sides, so there is no net water movement in either direction.

The consequences of these three conditions differ sharply between animal cells and plant cells, because plant cells have a rigid cell wall outside their plasma membrane and animal cells do not. Place a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution, such as distilled water, and water rushes in faster than it leaves; with no rigid wall to resist the swelling, the cell can burst, a process called hemolysis. Place that same red blood cell in a hypertonic solution, such as concentrated saltwater, and water leaves the cell faster than it enters, causing the cell to shrink and shrivel, a process called crenation.

A plant cell placed in the same hypotonic solution also takes in water and swells, but its rigid cell wall pushes back against the expanding plasma membrane, building up an internal pressure called turgor pressure that stops the cell from bursting and instead makes it firm, or turgid, which is actually the healthy, well-hydrated state for most plant cells and part of why well-watered plants stand upright. Place a plant cell in a hypertonic solution instead, and water leaves the cell fast enough that the plasma membrane pulls away from the surrounding cell wall entirely, a condition called plasmolysis, which causes wilting since the cell can no longer maintain firm structural pressure against its wall.

Much of this water movement is accelerated by aquaporins, the channel proteins covered in the membrane proteins and selective permeability chapters, which let water cross the membrane far faster than diffusion through the bilayer alone would allow, without letting solutes leak through the same channel. Osmosis is not a side issue for cells; it is a constant, ongoing physical pressure every cell must manage, which is exactly why maintaining the right internal solute balance, and thus the right direction and rate of osmosis, is one of the central jobs of a living cell's plasma membrane.
